config.title: Role-Based Route Protection

intro.title: Role-Based Route Protection
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Angular application that restricts access to certain routes based on a user's role. You will learn how to implement role-based route protection using Angular's built-in router guards. The core programming concept involves creating a custom guard service that checks a user's role before allowing navigation. You will work with TypeScript interfaces to define roles, Angular services to manage authentication state, and the CanActivate interface to secure routes. By the end, you'll have a functional guard that redirects users without the proper role to a safe page.
intro.usecase: Role-based route protection is a foundational security pattern in enterprise web applications. Developers implement it to control user access to different sections of a product, such as an admin dashboard, a customer portal, or internal reporting tools. For example, in a healthcare application, a doctor might see patient records and scheduling panels, while a receptionist only sees appointment forms and contact lists. This ensures users interact only with the UI components and data relevant to their permissions, maintaining security and a streamlined user experience.

objectives: Implement a role-based authentication service to manage user roles
Configure route guards to protect routes based on user roles
Apply role checks within route guard logic to control navigation
Integrate role-based route protection with Angular's routing module
Construct a user interface that conditionally renders navigation elements based on roles
Initialize and manage role state within Angular components
Bind role data to template logic for dynamic content display

steps.title: Import Angular Router and CommonModule
steps.instruction: In your AppModule (or feature module), import RouterModule and Routes from '@angular/router', and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.
steps.hint: You'll need to add these imports at the top of your module file. Use the import keyword followed by the module names and their source packages.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your module file will have the necessary imports for routing and common directives at the top, ready to be used in the imports array.
successCriteria: RouterModule and Routes are imported from '@angular/router', and CommonModule is imported from '@angular/common'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've imported all three: RouterModule and Routes from '@angular/router', and CommonModule from '@angular/common'. Check your import statements.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. Remember to import RouterModule and Routes from '@angular/router' for routing functionality, and CommonModule from '@angular/common' for basic directives.

steps.title: Define User Role Interface
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript interface called 'User' with a 'role' property of type string. Place this interface above the @NgModule decorator in your code.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and define the 'role' property with type 'string'.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a User interface with a role property that will be used later for role-based route protection.
successCriteria: A User interface is defined with a 'role' property of type string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've defined an interface named 'User' with a 'role' property of type 'string'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword and define a 'role' property with type 'string'.

steps.title: Create Auth Service with Role Property
steps.instruction: Create an AuthService class with a currentUser property of type User | null and methods to simulate login/logout with different roles.
steps.hint: Use the @Injectable decorator and define methods like login(role: UserRole) and logout() that update currentUser.
steps.expectedOutcome: An AuthService class is created with currentUser property and login/logout methods to manage user roles.
successCriteria: AuthService class exists with currentUser: User | null property, login(role: UserRole) method that sets currentUser, and logout() method that sets currentUser to null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created the AuthService, but check if you included all required methods and the currentUser property type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The AuthService is missing or incomplete. Ensure it has currentUser property and login/logout methods.

steps.title: Define Route Configuration with Data Property
steps.instruction: Inside the AppModule class, define a constant named 'routes' of type Routes array and add at least one route with a 'data' property containing a 'roles' array specifying allowed roles (e.g., ['admin']).
steps.hint: Use the Routes type imported earlier. Define routes as: const routes: Routes = [{ path: 'admin', component: AdminComponent, data: { roles: ['admin'] } }]; You can use a placeholder component name like 'AdminComponent' for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: A routes constant is defined with at least one route containing a data property that specifies allowed roles.
successCriteria: The code includes a 'routes' constant of type Routes with at least one route object containing a 'data' property with a 'roles' array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a 'routes' constant with the Routes type and included a 'data' property with 'roles' array in at least one route.
steps.feedbackWrong: The route configuration isn't complete. Define a constant named 'routes' with type Routes and add route objects with 'data' properties containing 'roles' arrays.

steps.title: Create Role Guard Service
steps.instruction: Create a new service called RoleGuard that implements the CanActivate interface. The service should check if the current user's role is included in the allowed roles defined in the route data.
steps.hint: Use the @Injectable decorator and implement the canActivate method. You'll need to inject AuthService and Router to access the current user and handle navigation.
steps.expectedOutcome: A RoleGuard service is created with the CanActivate interface implemented, ready to check user roles against route data.
successCriteria: RoleGuard service is defined with @Injectable decorator, implements CanActivate, and has a canActivate method that checks route data roles.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the service implements CanActivate and has the canActivate method.
steps.feedbackWrong: The RoleGuard service needs to implement CanActivate and include the canActivate method to check user roles.

steps.title: Inject AuthService in Role Guard
steps.instruction: In the RoleGuard service, inject the AuthService through the constructor to access the current user information.
steps.hint: Add a constructor parameter with type AuthService and assign it to a class property.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: injecting a service in a guard
constructor(private authService: AuthService) {}
steps.expectedOutcome: The RoleGuard service will have access to the AuthService instance through dependency injection.
successCriteria: RoleGuard constructor includes AuthService parameter and assigns it to a class property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added the AuthService parameter to the constructor and assigned it properly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The RoleGuard constructor doesn't have the AuthService injection. Review dependency injection in Angular services.

steps.title: Implement canActivate Method Logic
steps.instruction: Inside the RoleGuard service, implement the canActivate method to check if the current user exists and has the required role from the route's data property.
steps.hint: The canActivate method receives the route and state parameters. Access the required role via route.data['role'], then compare it with the current user's role from AuthService.
steps.expectedOutcome: The RoleGuard service now has a canActivate method that checks user authorization against route requirements.
successCriteria: The RoleGuard service contains a canActivate method that accesses route.data['role'] and compares it with the current user's role from AuthService.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the canActivate method needs to properly check the route's role data against the current user's role. Make sure you're accessing route.data['role'] and comparing it with this.authService.currentUser.role.
steps.feedbackWrong: The canActivate method implementation is missing or incorrect. Remember to check if the user exists and compare their role with the required role from the route's data property.

steps.title: Apply Guard to Route Configuration
steps.instruction: Add the RoleGuard to the 'canActivate' property of the admin route in your route configuration.
steps.hint: In the route configuration array, find the route with path 'admin' and add a 'canActivate' property with RoleGuard as its value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The admin route will now be protected by the RoleGuard, which will check the user's role before allowing access.
successCriteria: The 'admin' route in the routes array has a 'canActivate' property with RoleGuard as its value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added the 'canActivate' property to the admin route with RoleGuard as its value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The admin route should have a 'canActivate' property with RoleGuard as its value. Check the route configuration syntax.

steps.title: Create Login Component with Role Selection
steps.instruction: Create a LoginComponent class with a template that displays three buttons: 'Login as Admin', 'Login as User', and 'Login as Guest'.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator to define the component. The template should contain three button elements with appropriate labels.
steps.expectedOutcome: A LoginComponent class is created with a template containing three role selection buttons.
successCriteria: LoginComponent is defined with @Component decorator and template contains three button elements with labels for admin, user, and guest roles.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but make sure it has exactly three buttons with clear role labels (admin, user, guest).
steps.feedbackWrong: The component doesn't meet the requirements. Create a LoginComponent with three buttons for role selection.

steps.title: Create Protected and Public Components
steps.instruction: Create a public component named HomeComponent that returns a simple heading.
steps.hint: Define a new component class with @Component decorator and a template containing an <h2> element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A HomeComponent class is defined with a template that displays a heading.
successCriteria: HomeComponent is declared with @Component decorator and a template containing an <h2> element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure to use @Component decorator and include a template with an <h2> element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Review Angular component syntax: use @Component decorator with selector and template properties.

steps.title: Set Up Router Outlet in App Component
steps.instruction: Create an AppComponent class with a template containing a <router-outlet> element to display routed components.
steps.hint: The AppComponent should be declared in the AppModule and serve as the main container for your application's routed views.
steps.expectedOutcome: An AppComponent class is created with a template containing a <router-outlet> element, ready to display routed components.
successCriteria: AppComponent class is defined with @Component decorator, selector 'app-root', and template containing <router-outlet>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your AppComponent has both the @Component decorator with proper selector and template containing <router-outlet>.
steps.feedbackWrong: The AppComponent wasn't created correctly. Remember to define a class with @Component decorator, selector 'app-root', and template with <router-outlet> element.

steps.title: Test Role-Based Navigation
steps.instruction: In the AppComponent template, add navigation links for the 'home' and 'admin' routes, and display the current user role.
steps.hint: Use routerLink for navigation and bind to the authService.currentUser.role property to show the role.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example navigation template
Home Admin

Current role: {{ authService.currentUser?.role || 'none' }}
steps.expectedOutcome: The app will have navigation links to test the role-based guard and show the current user role.
successCriteria: The AppComponent template includes routerLink navigation for 'home' and 'admin' routes and displays the current user role.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some navigation elements, but make sure to include both 'home' and 'admin' links and display the current role from authService.
steps.feedbackWrong: The navigation links or role display are missing. Check that you're using routerLink for navigation and binding to authService.currentUser.role.
